name: Sciton Halo

card.summary: Halo is a hybrid fractional laser that pairs ablative and non-ablative wavelengths to smooth texture, shrink pores and reduce sun damage and fine lines.
card.aka: HALO by Sciton, Halo hybrid fractional laser
card.note: Clinician-performed laser treatment; laser resurfacing carries documented risks including scarring and pigment change.

quick.overview:
HALO is a laser made by Sciton that delivers two wavelengths together in the same treated zone: a 2940 nm ablative erbium wavelength that addresses the surface and a 1470 nm non-ablative wavelength that reaches deeper. The manufacturer says it targets fine lines and wrinkles, sun damage, pigment, scars, pores and vascular lesions.
The goal is smoother, clearer, more even-toned skin. Sciton says patients usually resume regular activity within 24 hours and that only topical anaesthetic is needed. Published trials on Sciton erbium lasers, which are related technology, report improvements in pigment and texture, though no trial of HALO itself has been published.
quick.how: A clinician treats the face with the laser after topical anaesthetic. Treatment depth is adjustable: the manufacturer lists 20 to 100 micrometres for the ablative wavelength and 250 to 700 for the non-ablative one. Skin shows redness and swelling afterwards, then results develop as the skin renews.
quick.risks: Laser resurfacing risks reported in the literature include scarring, pigment changes, acne and herpes reactivation. A paper on full-field erbium resurfacing identified complication rates by setting and proposed safety parameters. Choice of settings and clinician training influence outcomes.

lead: HALO by Sciton is described by its manufacturer as a hybrid fractional laser that combines a 2940 nm ablative wavelength and a 1470 nm non-ablative wavelength in the same treatment zone. It came to market in 2014.[1]

The two wavelengths work at different depths: the ablative one addresses the epidermis, texture and pores, while the non-ablative one reaches the dermis for deeper sun damage, collagen stimulation and pigment. Sciton lists fine lines, wrinkles, dyschromia, scars, pigmented lesions, pores and vascular lesions as targets, and says patients can usually resume regular activity within 24 hours.[1]

Wikipedia explains that ablative lasers such as the 2940 nm Er:YAG vaporise tissue, non-ablative lasers keep skin intact, and fractional lasers treat many pinpoints while leaving healthy skin between them. It notes heating the dermis stimulates fibroblasts to form new collagen and elastin.[2]

chain: Two laser wavelengths treat surface and deeper skin together
Old skin is removed and the dermis is stimulated to renew
Smoother texture, finer pores and more even tone
angle.text: HALO is used to resurface skin. The ablative wavelength refines surface texture and pores while the non-ablative one targets deeper sun damage and pigment, aiming for smoother, more even skin.

paras: Per the manufacturer, the ablative 2940 nm wavelength is tunable from 20 to 100 micrometres and the non-ablative 1470 nm wavelength from 250 to 700 micrometres.[1] The two are delivered together rather than in separate sessions.[1]

Wikipedia lists scarring, hyperpigmentation, acne and herpes as general laser-resurfacing risks, and says erbium and CO2 fractional systems have a better safety profile than older lasers.[2] A 2020 Aesthetic Surgery Journal study of full-field erbium YAG resurfacing reported complication rates and suggested safety parameters.[5]

No studies of HALO itself were found. Studies of Sciton erbium:YAG devices report relevant outcomes: a 2004 trial of single-pass Er:YAG in 20 patients with mild to moderate photodamage reported 58% reduction in pigment irregularities and 54% improvement in skin texture, with 3 to 5 days of redness and swelling and return to work within about 3 days.[3]

A 2007 study of 15 subjects combining very superficial Er:YAG peels with broadband light on a Sciton Profile system found significant improvement in photodamaged skin, greatest in overall appearance and pigment, largely maintained at three months.[4]

timeline.event: Trial of single-pass erbium:YAG for photodamage published.[3]
